questions.q: When is the ultimate time to pull the goalie?
questions.headline: Down one, anywhere from 2:20 to 4:40 left; down two, about 3:45. Most teams wait too long, but it costs less than you'd think.
body: With an extra skater, a team down one late scored 7.4 goals per 60 minutes but allowed 21.7 into the empty net; with the goalie in, 2.4 for and 2.4 against.

Feeding those rates into a second-by-second model, the chance of tying a one-goal game is highest (42.5%) when the goalie comes out with 2:20 to 4:40 left: a wide, flat top. NHL teams typically pulled at 1:45, which gets 42.0%. Never pulling gets 40.2%.
Down two, the best time is about 3:45 left (14.0% to tie vs 13.9% at the usual 2:33). The empty-net goals against cost little: losing by two counts the same as losing by one.

chart.title: Chance to tie a one-goal game, by when the goalie is pulled

questions.method: Third periods of 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular-season games. Goal rates for teams trailing by one (and two) measured at 5-on-5 with the goalie in and 6-on-5 with it pulled, then a second-by-second model of the race to a tying goal for every possible pull time. Assumes rates don't change with the clock; a goal against ends the chase.

questions.q: How much do faceoff wins actually matter?
questions.headline: A little. Going from 50% to 55% on faceoffs is worth about 0.9 goals a season.
body: In the 30 seconds after a 5-on-5 faceoff, the winner's goal difference is +1.9 per 100 wins in the offensive zone, +0.3 at center and -0.3 in its own zone (still deep in its end, a win only limits the damage).
Spread over a season, a team winning 55% instead of 50% gains roughly 0.9 goals (about 0.1 wins). Across team-seasons, faceoff percentage and goal share correlate at r = 0.28.
The edge is real but short-lived: after half a minute, possession has usually changed hands several times.

chart.title: Goal edge for the faceoff winner in the next 30 seconds (per 100 wins, 5-on-5)

questions.method: Every 5-on-5 faceoff in 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular seasons: goals for minus against for the winning team until the next faceoff or 30 seconds, by zone (zone from the winner's side). Season estimate assumes ~58 faceoffs a game, 62% at 5-on-5.

questions.q: Do fights change the momentum of a game?
questions.headline: Not measurably. Teams losing the shot battle before a fight recover about as much as they do without one.
body: Before a fight, the team losing the shot battle had 38.5% of attempts over the previous 10 minutes. In the 10 minutes after, it had 50.5%.

That looks like a momentum swing, but random moments with the same starting share bounce back just as much (to 49.8%), because lopsided stretches rarely last. The fight's own effect: +0.7 points (90% range -0.2 to +1.6).
So the swing fans see after a fight is mostly regression to the mean, not the fight.

chart.title: Shot-attempt share of the team that was behind, next 10 minutes

questions.method: Fighting majors in 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular seasons (5th to 50th minute). Shot attempts (goals, shots, misses, blocks) 10 minutes before and after. Expected = what random non-fight moments in the same games did from the same starting share (a linear fit), so regression to the mean is removed.

questions.q: Is a two-goal lead the worst lead in hockey?
questions.headline: No. Teams that went up two won 87% of the time, vs 69% after going up one.
body: Once a team led by one, it won 68.7% of those games. Once it led by two, 87.3%. By three, 96.4%.
The 'worst lead' line comes from how a blown two-goal lead feels: the comeback gets remembered and the many routine wins don't. Every extra goal of cushion raised the chance of winning.

chart.title: Won the game after first leading by…

questions.method: Every regular-season game in 2023-24 through 2025-26: the first time each team led by 1, 2 or 3 goals in regulation, and whether it won (including overtime and shootouts).
questions.sample: 5,307 one-goal leads, 3,338 two-goal leads, 1,962 three-goal leads

questions.q: Is the NHL a "First to Three" league?
questions.headline: The first team to three goals won 88.1% of those games.
body: Across 3,936 completed regular-season games, 3,450 had a team reach three goals in regulation or overtime. That team won 3,039 times and lost 411 times.
In 486 games, neither team reached three before a shootout. Those games are excluded from the win-rate calculation; a shootout-deciding goal does not count as reaching three.
Three goals is a useful milestone, not a guarantee or a causal rule. Teams that score three first are already leading, and stronger teams reach that mark more often.

chart.title: Outcome for the first team to three goals

questions.method: Walk actual goals chronologically in each 2023–24 through 2025–26 regular-season game. Identify the first team to score its third goal in regulation or overtime, then check the eventual winner, including shootouts. Exclude shootout attempts and games where neither team reaches three.
questions.sample: 3,450 qualifying games out of 3,936 completed games

questions.q: How much does a back-to-back hurt?
questions.headline: About 7 points of win probability: tired teams won 41% against rested ones, vs 48% expected.
body: On the second night of a back-to-back against a team that had rested, teams won 41.5% of the time. From their records in rested games and home ice, we'd have expected 48.2%.
The gap is -6.8 points (90% range -9.5 to -3.9), worth about 0.14 standings points per game. Part of it is the backup goalie who usually starts those nights.

chart.title: Win rate on the second night of a back-to-back vs a rested team

questions.method: 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular seasons. A back-to-back = played the day before; the opponent had at least one day off. Expected = each team's win rate in its rested games (lightly shrunk) combined with the opponent's and league home-ice advantage (log5).

questions.q: Does an intermission make a power play less dangerous?
questions.headline: After the break, scoring pace is 26% lower than uninterrupted power plays at the same stage.
body: After an intermission, these 5-on-4 power plays scored at 0.187 goals per two minutes of power-play time. Uninterrupted power plays, weighted to the same elapsed penalty time, scored at 0.252.

The relative difference is -26.1% (90% game-bootstrap range -38.9% to -13.0%). Only time after the break is counted for the split power plays; this is a scoring pace, not the chance a full power play scores.

A carryover power play has already survived without scoring before the horn. Comparing with the same stage of uninterrupted power plays helps account for that. Team quality, score, period and faceoff location are not matched, so this comparison cannot establish that the intermission caused the difference.

chart.title: Scoring pace: goals per 2 minutes of 5-on-4 time

questions.method: 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular-season NHL play-by-play. Clean two-minute minors from 5-on-5 to 5-on-4, both goalies present. Carryovers start in the final 119 seconds of period 1 or 2; only their next-period exposure and goals count. Controls fit entirely within one regulation period. Stop at a power-play goal, another penalty, a strength/goalie change or 120 elapsed game seconds. Count exposure and goals in 15-second elapsed-penalty bins; weight uninterrupted scoring rates by carryover exposure in each bin. 90% percentile intervals resample games 1,000 times (seed 42). Descriptive, not causal.
questions.sample: 3,936 games; 995 carryover power plays with post-break exposure, 91 post-break goals, 975.7 post-break minutes; 14,102 uninterrupted power plays

questions.q: How much does scoring first matter?
questions.headline: A lot: the team that scored first won 67% of games.
body: Scoring first, home teams won 69.9% and road teams 63.1%.
Timing matters: an opening goal in the first period led to a win 65.2% of the time; when the first goal came in the third, 79.6%.
Part of this is selection: better teams score first more often. But a one-goal head start is a real edge in a low-scoring game.

chart.title: Won the game after scoring first

questions.method: Every 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular-season game with a goal in regulation or overtime: did the team that scored first win (including overtime and shootouts)?

questions.q: How often does the team leading after two periods win?
questions.headline: 85% of the time. Up one: 75%. Up two: 91%. Up three or more: 98%.
body: Teams ahead after 40 minutes won 85.2% of games. A one-goal lead held 74.8% of the time, two goals 91.0%, three or more 97.8%.
Games tied after two went to overtime 38.5% of the time.

chart.title: Won the game when leading after two periods by…

questions.method: Score after 40 minutes in every 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular-season game and the final result (overtime and shootouts included).

questions.q: What's the most dangerous kind of shot?
questions.headline: Anything from right on top of the goalie: 14% of shots within 10 feet go in, twice the average. Next: rebound (11%).
body: Of unblocked shots, 6.6% became goals. Within 10 ft shots went in 13.6% of the time, rebound 11.3%, 10 to 20 ft 10.8%.

A rebound from under 20 feet goes in 13.1% of the time. Distance dominates everything else, which is why our expected-goals model leans on it first, then on rebounds and how the puck moved just before the shot. (The play-by-play has no passes, so one-timers and cross-ice feeds can only be inferred.)
The least dangerous: from the point (over 50 ft) (1.3%).

chart.title: Share of unblocked shots that became goals

questions.method: Unblocked, non-empty-net regulation shots in 2023-24 through 2025-26 (NHL play-by-play). Categories overlap (a rebound can also be from close in). Rebound = a shot within 3 seconds of the same team's previous shot; rush = within 4 seconds of an event in the neutral or defensive zone.

questions.q: How much of a goalie's season is luck?
questions.headline: Most of it: roughly 69–81% of the spread between goalies in one season is luck.
body: For goalies facing 1,000+ unblocked shots, the differences in goals saved above expected are what you'd see if 81% of them came from chance (which shots happened to go in), not skill.
The share is 76% for goalies with 500+ shots and 69% for workhorses with 1,500+ (a smaller, more selected group, so the estimates bounce around). Either way, luck is the bigger part.
That's why our player values shrink goalie results hard toward average, and why one great season predicts the next one only weakly (year-to-year correlation about 0.14).

chart.title: Share of the goalie spread that's luck, by shots faced

questions.method: MoneyPuck goalie seasons 2022-23 to 2025-26, all situations. Luck share = the average binomial variance of goals saved above expected per shot (from each goalie's own expected save rate and shot count) divided by the observed variance across goalies.

questions.q: When does a power play actually score?
questions.headline: Not early. The first 15 seconds are the slowest; after that the pace is steady to the end.
body: Scoring pace in the first 15 seconds of a 5-on-4: 0.20 goals per two minutes, -17% vs the power play's average (0.24). From 30 seconds on it stays within a narrow band; the busiest slice is 45–60s.
The first 30 seconds produce 25% of power-play goals while taking up 29% of power-play time. The opening faceoff has to be won and the set-up established before the chances come.
Overall, 19.4% of these power plays scored.

chart.title: Power-play scoring pace by time into a 5-on-4 (goals per 2 minutes)

questions.method: Two-minute minors that created a 5-on-4 in 2023-24 through 2025-26 regular seasons (not in the last minute). Time on the power play and power-play goals counted in 15-second slices until a goal, two minutes, or a change in strength.

questions.q: Does it make sense to pay a lot of goalies and should you sign them long term?
questions.headline: Pay for a proven record, but keep it short. A top goalie keeps about 25% of his edge the next season and almost none of it by year three.
body: Take goalies whose last three seasons rank in the top fifth: +5.1 goals saved above expected per 1,000 shots. The next season, the same goalies average +1.3; year two +0.8; year three +0.3; year five -1.1.

For a starter facing about 2,500 shots, that record is worth about 2.1 wins a season, which is star money. What the next season actually delivers is closer to 0.5 wins. A short deal pays for the part that lasts; years four to eight of a long deal pay for a record that no longer predicts anything.

This season's 13 goalie deals of $5M+ that have a full season behind them: 7 saved fewer goals per 1,000 shots after signing than in the two seasons before, averaging +3.7 before and +2.2 since. Biggest drop: Adin Hill (+4.2 to -10.8); best: Philipp Grubauer (-6.5 to +3.1).

Paying a goalie isn't wasted: a good starter still beats a bad one. The trap is paying for one hot stretch, and for years of it. Most of one goalie season is luck, which is why the record fades (see the question on goalie luck).

chart.title: Top-fifth goalies: goals saved per 1,000 shots, record vs each later season

questions.method: MoneyPuck goalie seasons 2008-09 through 2025-26, all situations; goals saved above expected (expected goals minus goals) per 1,000 unblocked shots. Record = three straight seasons totaling 3,000+ shots; top fifth = +3.2 or better. Later seasons count when he faced 1,000+ shots, so goalies who lost the job drop out and the later years flatter the group. Wins at 6 goals per win. Deals: current contracts (public terms) of $5M+ a season, completed seasons only.
questions.sample: 793 three-season records; 131 top-fifth records with a next season, 61 with a fifth; 13 current deals

questions.q: Does living in a low-tax state let a team sign players for cheaper cap hits?
questions.headline: A little: teams in no-income-tax states sign comparable players for about 9% less. But it doesn't track the tax rate: high-tax states and Canada pay no more than the rest, so taxes are at most part of the story.
body: We priced 1,885 contracts that today's players signed since 2012 against what contracts like them usually cost (same WAR before signing, age, position, term, free-agent status and season). Teams outside Florida, Texas, Tennessee, Nevada and Washington paid 9% more for the same contract (90% range +5% to +13%). By group: middle-tax US teams +11%, high-tax US teams +6%, Canadian teams +11%.

If players priced taxes in fully, the gap would be far bigger: to keep the same top-dollar take-home as in Florida, a player would need about 27% more in California and 36% more in Ontario (somewhat less once road-game taxes are counted, since players pay some tax wherever they play). Instead, each 10 points of top tax rate goes with only +3% (90% range -1% to +6%). High-tax US teams even pay less of a premium than middle-tax ones.

Is it winning instead? Several no-tax teams are recent contenders players want to join (Florida, Tampa Bay, Vegas, Dallas), and strong teams do pay less, about 3% per 10 points of last season's points percentage. But allowing for that the no-tax gap is still +8% (90% range +5% to +11%), and leaving out any one no-tax team keeps it between +8% and +10%. For unrestricted free agents choosing a new team (531 signings), where a tax break should matter most, it is +11%.

So: a modest discount, about the size of the normal spread between teams' spending habits (±6%), that comes with having no state income tax but doesn't grow with the tax gap. That's an association, not proof that taxes cause it; the location, climate and team culture of these six teams travel with the tax break. Players' real tax bills depend on where they live, road games and how deals are structured with signing bonuses, none of which is in this data.

chart.title: Cap hit for the same contract vs teams in no-income-tax states

questions.method: CapWages contract history (licensed) for current NHL players: standard contracts signed July 2012 onward, entry-level and two-way deals excluded. Market value: least-squares fit of log cap hit on WAR per 82 games over the three completed seasons before signing (our WAR-lite, weights 1/.7/.45, 25 games of replacement-level prior; piecewise, separately for pending UFAs), age, position, term and first-season dummies (the cap's growth). Tax groups by the signing team: no state income tax (FL, TX, TN, NV, WA), high-tax US (state top rate 9% or more: CA, NY, NJ, MN, MA, DC), Canada, and the rest. Rates (new source): Tax Foundation 2026 state top rates plus the 37% federal rate; BDO Canada Tax Facts 2026 combined federal and provincial top rates; city taxes and road-game taxes left out; 2026 rates applied to every year. 90% ranges from 999 bootstrap resamples of signing teams (contracts from one team aren't independent). The fit explains 79% of the spread in cap hits. Only players on NHL contracts today are covered, so older deals of players who have since left are missing.
questions.sample: 1,885 contracts: 356 by 6 no-tax teams, 576 by 10 high-tax US teams, 407 by 7 Canadian teams, 546 by 10 others

questions.q: What is more valuable: one Connor McDavid, or Leon Draisaitl and Evan Bouchard together?
questions.headline: Draisaitl and Bouchard, by about 3.4 wins a season. But they cost $12.0M more against the cap, and that money spent on another player makes it close to even.
body: Over the last three seasons, per 82 games: McDavid 6.2 wins above replacement, Draisaitl 5.4, Bouchard 4.1. Together the pair is worth 9.5, 3.4 more than McDavid alone. Our second method (RAPM, which credits each player for what happens on the ice while he plays, after allowing for teammates and opponents) agrees: McDavid 5.3, the pair 7.7.

Looking ahead, our career forecast for this season and next has McDavid at 12.1 WAR and Draisaitl and Bouchard at 16.7 combined. Allowing for injuries and ordinary ups and downs, McDavid comes out ahead in about 10% of outcomes (treating the players as independent).

Cost changes the answer. This season McDavid's cap hit is $12.5M; Draisaitl's and Bouchard's add up to $24.5M, $12.0M more. Players paid about $12.0M produce a median 2.5 WAR per 82 (middle half 1.7 to 3.4; 19 players). McDavid plus one of them is worth about 8.7, close to the pair's 9.5: for the same cap money it's roughly a tie, with McDavid's side slightly behind.

What WAR can't see: one player can only be on the ice about 22 minutes a night, so two stars cover more of the game, and the pair lets a team spread its talent across two lines and the blue line. In McDavid's favor, the highest-end players may matter more in the playoffs, which this measure doesn't test. Both views are estimates from regular-season results.

chart.title: Wins above replacement per 82 games, last three seasons
x: McDavid + a player at that cap gap

questions.method: Our WAR-lite player values (three seasons weighted 1/.7/.45, 25 games of replacement-level prior; RAPM version beside it). Forecast: the experimental career-curve model (mean and 10th-90th percentile range per season, summed over 2026-27 and 2027-28; spreads combined as independent normals). Cap hits: public contract terms for 2026-27. Going rate: median WAR per 82 of non-entry-level players with 100+ games over three seasons and a cap hit within $1.5M of the gap.
questions.sample: 3 players, 476 games over three seasons; 19 players at the cap gap

questions.headline: Yes, but it is smaller than it looks: points percentage jumps from 45.1% to 54.9% after a mid-season change, and about 59% of that jump would have happened anyway. The rest is worth about 7 standings points over 82 games.
body: In 53 mid-season changes since 2008-09, teams earned 45.1% of available points under the old coach and 54.9% under the new one. Teams that kept their coach through an equally bad start also bounced back, to 50.9% on average: bad stretches end on their own. The new-coach teams beat that by 4.1 percentage points (90% range 1.7 to 6.3), about 6.7 standings points per 82 games.

When it shows up: first 10 games 3.0 percentage points above expected (90% range -1.2 to 7.4), games 11-25 4.8, game 26 on 3.7. It does not fade quickly. 64% of the changes beat their expected pace for the rest of the season, so plenty don't.

The next full season, teams that changed coaches finished 1.4 percentage points above what their season before predicts (90% range -0.3 to 3.1), so any lasting effect is small and can't be told apart from zero.

This is an association, not a clean test of coaching. Teams that fire a coach often change other things at the same time: trades, call-ups, a different starting goalie, a healthier lineup. With 53 changes the range is wide; a bump of zero is outside it.

chart.title: After a mid-season coaching change: points % above teams that kept their coach (percentage points)

questions.method: Regular seasons 2008-09 through 2025-26 except 2012-13, 2019-20 and 2020-21 (NHL schedules and coach records). A change is a new coach's first game with at least 10 games before and after it. Expected = a straight-line fit of later points % on earlier points % among team-seasons with no change, split at the same game (regression to the mean). 90% ranges: bootstrap over changes. Next season: points % vs a fit of next season on this season among teams without a change.
questions.sample: 53 mid-season changes; 388 team-seasons without one; 36 with a next season

questions.q: Is a first overall pick better than two picks between 5th and 10th overall?
questions.headline: Yes, on average: two picks from 5th to 10th bring about 13.4 wins above replacement in their first seven or eight seasons to the No. 1 pick's 20.4. But the No. 1 pick is a franchise player 53% of the time, and two later picks give you one only 7% of the time.
body: Across the 15 drafts from 2005-2019 whose players have finished their first seven or eight NHL seasons, the No. 1 pick averaged 20.4 WAR in that window (median 21.0). Picks 5 through 10 averaged 6.7 (median 5.1), so two of them add up to 13.4. The No. 1 pick's edge over the pair is 7.0 WAR (90% range 2.7 to 11.3): fifteen No. 1 picks is a small sample, and McDavid alone moves the average.

Pick by pick: a real No. 1 pick beat the combined value of a random pair of 5-10 picks 72% of the time. The 5-10 group is lopsided, a few stars and many middling players, so the typical pair (median) is worth 12.2, less than twice the average.

Stars are where the top pick earns its keep. 53% of No. 1 picks reached 20+ WAR in the window, a franchise player; 3% of 5-10 picks did, so two of them give you one about 7% of the time. Best No. 1 pick: Connor McDavid (36.7); worst: Nail Yakupov (2.3).

One caution: our smoothed value curve, which pools each slot with its neighbors to cut noise, puts the No. 1 slot at only 11.8 and two picks from 5 to 10 at 13.6. Smoothing can't show a jump at No. 1, and fifteen picks can't prove one, so the true gap is somewhere between the two. A single star is also hard to find any other way, which is part of why teams rarely trade the No. 1 pick for two later ones. The window covers players' cheap early years, which are when a pick pays off most.

chart.title: Wins above replacement in the first 7-8 NHL seasons after the draft

questions.method: Our draft-value model: WAR-lite in the first 7 seasons after the draft for forwards and 8 for defensemen (goalies 9), each season floored at 0, for drafts whose window is complete (2005-2019). Franchise player = 20+ WAR in the window. Pair comparison: every No. 1 pick against every pair of 5-10 picks. 90% range: bootstrap over picks.
questions.sample: 15 first overall picks, 88 picks from 5th to 10th

questions.q: Should you draft goalies high in the draft?
questions.headline: Probably not: goalie value drops off much less after the first round than skater value does. A first-round goalie has given about 2x what a goalie from rounds 2-3 gives; a first-round skater about 6x a skater from those rounds. So a skater first and a goalie later has beaten the reverse, narrowly: the 90% range includes a tie.
body: Since 2005, teams took 18 goalies in the first round. In their first 9 seasons they averaged 0.76 wins above replacement a season; goalies from rounds 2 and 3 averaged 0.36 (93 goalies). For skaters the same drop is from 0.66 to 0.11 (450 and 825 skaters). Waiting a round costs a team much less at goalie. (Goalie and skater WAR aren't on quite the same scale, since the floor at zero flatters high-variance goalies, so compare each position's drop rather than the levels.)

Put together, a first-round skater plus a goalie from rounds 2-3 has been worth 0.16 more WAR a season than a first-round goalie plus a skater from rounds 2-3 (90% range -0.25 to 0.53). Even reaching the NHL is less certain: 44% of first-round goalies played 200+ NHL games, against 69% of first-round skaters. First-rounders were 6% of the drafted goalies with a finished window and produced 21% of their value.
Of the 23 goalies starting at least half of their team's games now, 3 were first-round picks, 7 came from rounds 2-3, 10 from round 4 or later, and 3 went undrafted.

Why: goalies develop late, often not settling in the NHL until their mid-20s, and one goalie season is mostly luck, so it's hard to tell the best 18-year-olds apart. High picks do hit (Carey Price, Andrei Vasilevskiy, Jake Oettinger), but there are only 18 first-round goalies to learn from, so the ranges are wide. The pattern, not proof: teams that want a goalie have usually done better finding one later.

chart.title: Wins above replacement per season in the first years after the draft

questions.method: Our draft-value model: WAR-lite in the first 9 seasons after the draft for goalies, 7 for forwards and 8 for defensemen, each season floored at 0, divided by the window's length so positions compare per season; drafts 2005-2019 (complete windows only). Played = 200+ career NHL games. Goalie WAR is saves above average, shrunk toward average, and the 0 floor flatters high-variance goalies, so goalie and skater levels don't compare exactly; the drop-off from the first round within each position does. Starters: started half or more of their team's games over the last three seasons. 90% range: bootstrap over picks.
questions.sample: 281 drafted goalies (18 in the first round, 93 in rounds 2-3), 1,275 skaters in rounds 1-3; 23 current starters
